SDK migration¶

bigdata-client and bigdata-research-tools are removed. Use REST (BIGDATA_API_KEY) / bigdata-smart-batching / OpenAI. Pass company CSVs (RP_ENTITY_ID, COMPANY_NAME) instead of watchlists. See Thematic_Screener_CLI and MIGRATION_PATTERNS.md.

⚠️ SDK Migration Notice¶

This notebook has been migrated off bigdata-client and bigdata-research-tools.

  • Use src/bigdata_rest.py and src/search_helper.py for API access
  • Company universes are now CSV files with RP_ENTITY_ID and COMPANY_NAME columns (no more SDK watchlists)
  • RiskLabeler replaced with SimpleLabeler - advanced entity sentiment features removed
  • Risk tree generation now requires custom logic
  • See README.md for updated setup instructions

Analyzing Spillover Risks from Rising Bond Spreads in Western Europe¶

Why It Matters¶

Understanding how countries are exposed to financial contagion and spillover effects from rising bond spreads is critical for sovereign risk assessment and macroeconomic stability analysis. As bond yields diverge and sovereign debt costs increase, policymakers and analysts must proactively assess exposure to financial market tensions, fiscal pressures, and potential contagion effects across Western European nations.

What It Does¶

The RiskAnalyzer class, part of the bigdata-research-tools package, is purpose-built to meet this challenge. Designed for risk analysts, portfolio managers, and investment professionals, it systematically analyzes entity exposure to specific risk channels using unstructured data from news, earnings calls, and regulatory filings.

How It Works¶

RiskAnalyzer combines hybrid semantic search, risk factor taxonomies, and structured validation techniques to deliver:

  • Targeted extraction of risk signals and supporting evidence from massive unstructured datasets
  • Standardized exposure metrics to compare risk across different countries
  • Actionable insights that inform investment strategies and sovereign bond positioning decisions
  • Time-based monitoring to track how exposure levels shift in response to bond market developments

A Real-World Use Case¶

This cookbook illustrates the full workflow through a practical example: identifying Western European countries facing spillover risks from rising bond spreads. You'll learn how to convert unstructured narrative (news articles) into structured, quantifiable sovereign risk intelligence, tracking bond market pressures across Germany, France, Italy, Spain, and other European nations.

Async Compatibility Setup¶

Run this cell first - Required for Google Colab, Jupyter Notebooks, and VS Code with Jupyter extension:

Why is this needed?¶

Interactive environments (Colab, Jupyter) already have an asyncio event loop running. When bigdata-research-tools makes async API calls (like to OpenAI), you'll get this error without nest_asyncio:

RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop

The nest_asyncio.apply() command patches this to allow nested event loops.

💡 Tip: If you're unsure which environment you're in, just run the cell below - it won't hurt in any environment!

In [1]:
%load_ext autoreload
%autoreload 2
In [2]:
import datetime
start = datetime.datetime.now()

try:
    import asyncio
    asyncio.get_running_loop()
    import nest_asyncio; nest_asyncio.apply()
    print("✅ nest_asyncio applied")
except (RuntimeError, ImportError):
    print("✅ nest_asyncio not needed or not available")

✅ nest_asyncio applied

Defining Your Risk Analysis Parameters¶

To perform a sovereign risk analysis, we need to define several key parameters:

  • Main Theme (main_theme): The risk scenario to analyze (e.g. Spillovers from Rising Bond Spreads in Western Europe)
  • Focus (analyst_focus): The analyst focus that provides an expert perspective on the scenario and helps break it down into risks
  • Entity Universe (dict_country_bank, entities_countries, entities_banks): Western European countries plus their central banks. Countries are the primary entities scored in the analysis; central banks are searched separately to maximize coverage, then mapped back to their country.
  • Time Period (start_date and end_date): The date range over which to run the search
  • Document Type / Scope (document_type): Which document categories to search over (news, filings, transcripts, all) -- passed to bigdata-smart-batching's category filter
  • Model Selection (llm_model): The LLM model used to label the search result chunks
  • Removed/not reimplemented after the SDK migration: sources, fiscal_year, rerank_threshold, and control-entity co-mention filtering are not exposed by the REST search helpers in src/.
In [9]:
# ===== Theme Definition =====
main_theme = "Spillovers from Rising Bond Spreads in Western Europe"
analyst_focus = (
    "Generate a mind map of current and future risks that western european countries "
    "can face as a result of rising bond spreads."
)

# ===== Entity Universe (Western Europe countries + central banks) =====
universe_path = "data/western_europe_countries_banks.csv"
countries_df, banks_df, dict_country_bank, id_to_country = load_sovereign_universe(universe_path)

entities_countries = countries_df["RP_ENTITY_ID"].tolist()
entities_banks = banks_df["RP_ENTITY_ID"].tolist()
id_to_name_countries = dict(zip(countries_df["RP_ENTITY_ID"], countries_df["ENTITY_NAME"]))
id_to_name_banks = dict(zip(banks_df["RP_ENTITY_ID"], banks_df["ENTITY_NAME"]))

control_entities = None  # control-entity co-mention filtering not exposed by the REST search helper

# ===== LLM Specification =====
llm_model = "gpt-5.6-luna"

# ===== Docs Configuration =====
document_type = "news"
fiscal_year = None

# ===== Specify Time Range =====
start_date = "2025-07-01"
end_date = "2025-10-03"

print(f"Countries: {list(id_to_name_countries.values())}")
print(f"Central banks: {list(id_to_name_banks.values())}")
print(f"Date range: {start_date} to {end_date}")

Define a Risk Taxonomy¶

The original notebook used bigdata-research-tools' LLM-powered RiskAnalyzer.generate_risk_tree to mind-map the theme into a taxonomy tree. That functionality was removed with the SDK and is not reimplemented here -- src/entity_risk_prompt_labeler.generate_risk_tree intentionally still raises NotImplementedError. Instead we define a small, predefined taxonomy of sovereign bond-spillover sub-themes aligned with the Western European country universe.

In [10]:
# generate_risk_tree() (bigdata-research-tools) is removed and NOT reimplemented
# (src/entity_risk_prompt_labeler.generate_risk_tree raises NotImplementedError
# by design -- calling it would stop the notebook here). We use a small
# predefined taxonomy instead of an LLM-generated mind map.

taxonomy = {
    "sovereign_refinancing_risk": (
        "Rising sovereign bond spreads increase refinancing costs and rollover risk "
        "for Western European government debt."
    ),
    "fiscal_sustainability_pressure": (
        "Widening sovereign spreads signal mounting fiscal sustainability pressures "
        "across Western European countries."
    ),
    "financial_contagion_spillover": (
        "Cross-border financial contagion from rising bond spreads threatens "
        "macroeconomic stability in Western Europe."
    ),
}
for label, summary in taxonomy.items():
    print(f"- {label}: {summary}")

- sovereign_refinancing_risk: Rising sovereign bond spreads increase refinancing costs and rollover risk for Western European government debt.
- fiscal_sustainability_pressure: Widening sovereign spreads signal mounting fiscal sustainability pressures across Western European countries.
- financial_contagion_spillover: Cross-border financial contagion from rising bond spreads threatens macroeconomic stability in Western Europe.

Each taxonomy entry is a descriptive sentence that explicitly connects the sub-theme back to the main theme, ensuring search results remain contextually relevant, and doubles as the smart-batching search query text for that sub-theme.

In [11]:
labels = list(taxonomy.keys())
node_summaries = list(taxonomy.values())
In [12]:
node_summaries
Out[12]:
['Rising sovereign bond spreads increase refinancing costs and rollover risk for Western European government debt.',
 'Widening sovereign spreads signal mounting fiscal sustainability pressures across Western European countries.',
 'Cross-border financial contagion from rising bond spreads threatens macroeconomic stability in Western Europe.']

Retrieve Content using Bigdata’s Search Capabilities¶

With the taxonomy and screening parameters defined, we use bigdata-smart-batching (via src/search_helper.run_universe_search) to plan and execute the search. Two parameters control cost:

  • Chunk Percentage (chunk_percentage): The fraction of the estimated relevant chunks to actually retrieve (kept at 1-2% for cost control).
  • Requests Per Minute (requests_per_minute): Rate limit for the underlying search execution.

The original notebook ran two searches: one over Western European countries and one over their central banks. Bank hits are mapped back to the parent country before scoring.

In [13]:
# bigdata-smart-batching search parameters (cost control: small sample).
chunk_percentage = 0.05       # fraction of expected chunks to actually retrieve
requests_per_minute = 350

Retrieve news content for Western European countries, screened against the bond-spillover taxonomy defined above.

In [14]:
df_sentences_countries = search_by_entities(
    entities=entities_countries,
    sentences=node_summaries,
    start_date=start_date,
    end_date=end_date,
    id_to_name=id_to_name_countries,
    scope=document_type,
    chunk_percentage=chunk_percentage,
    requests_per_minute=requests_per_minute,
)
df_sentences_countries = df_sentences_countries.rename(columns={"sentiment": "bigdata_sentiment"})
df_sentences_countries = df_sentences_countries.loc[df_sentences_countries["entity_id"] != ""].copy()
df_sentences_countries["Country"] = df_sentences_countries["entity_name"]
print(f"Retrieved {len(df_sentences_countries)} country-attributed chunks")
df_sentences_countries.head()

Map central-bank hits back to their parent country (same pattern as the original SDK notebook), then merge with the country search so all scoring is at country level.

In [15]:
df_sentences_banks = search_by_entities(
    entities=entities_banks,
    sentences=node_summaries,
    start_date=start_date,
    end_date=end_date,
    id_to_name=id_to_name_banks,
    scope=document_type,
    chunk_percentage=chunk_percentage,
    requests_per_minute=requests_per_minute,
)
df_sentences_banks = df_sentences_banks.rename(columns={"sentiment": "bigdata_sentiment"})
df_sentences_banks = df_sentences_banks.loc[df_sentences_banks["entity_id"] != ""].copy()

# Original join: bank name -> country name, then concat at country level
df_sentences_banks_mapped = df_sentences_banks.copy()
reverse_dict = {v: k for k, v in dict_country_bank.items()}
df_sentences_banks_mapped["entity_name"] = df_sentences_banks_mapped["entity_name"].map(reverse_dict)
df_sentences_banks_mapped["Country"] = df_sentences_banks_mapped["entity_name"]

print(f"Mapped {len(df_sentences_banks_mapped)} bank chunks to countries")
df_sentences_banks_mapped[["entity_name", "Country", "entity_id", "headline"]].head()

Combine country and central-bank evidence, deduplicate overlapping chunks at country level, and cap rows for LLM labeling.

In [16]:
df_combined = pd.concat(
    [df_sentences_banks_mapped, df_sentences_countries],
    ignore_index=True,
)
# Prefer a stable chunk key when sentence_id is unavailable (REST search helper)
dedupe_cols = ["entity_name", "document_id", "chunk_text"]
df_combined = df_combined.drop_duplicates(subset=dedupe_cols, keep="first")

MAX_LABELING_ROWS = 10_000
if len(df_combined) > MAX_LABELING_ROWS:
    df_combined = (
        df_combined.sort_values("timestamp", ascending=False)
        .head(MAX_LABELING_ROWS)
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )

print(
    f"{len(df_combined)} country-level rows queued for labeling "
    f"(countries={df_combined['entity_name'].nunique()})"
)
df_combined["entity_name"].value_counts().head(10)

Label the Results¶

Use an LLM to analyze each text chunk and determine its relevance to the sub-themes. Any chunks which aren't explicitly linked to our main theme will be filtered out.

In [17]:
df_labeled = label_search_results(
    df_sentences=df_combined,
    terminal_labels=labels,
    main_theme=main_theme,
    model=llm_model,
)

df_labels = post_process_dataframe(df_labeled, extra_columns=["Country"])
df_labels.head()

Assess Thematic Exposure Across Your Entities¶

The function get_scored_df will calculate the composite thematic score, summing up the scores across the sub-themes for each entity (df_entity).

Identify Peak Coverage and Sentiment Windows¶

Identifies time windows of maximum media coverage and most negative sentiment for each entity, useful for analyzing critical risk moments.

        daily_sentiment, df_labels, sentiment_col="Sent_Rolling_30Days", min_max="min", lookback_days=30
    )
else:
    peak_coverage_windows, peak_coverage_data = {}, {}
    print("No daily sentiment data -- skipping narrative window detection.")

Peak Volume Narrative - Date: 26-08-2025¶

France is receiving negative refinancing-related coverage primarily because fiscal deterioration and political instability are driving higher sovereign and corporate funding costs, with potential knock-on effects for real estate borrowers rather than because of a reported property-specific default. Coverage on 26 August 2025 highlighted a 10-year French yield of 3.51% and an OAT-Bund spread of 75 basis points, while UBS cited a 5.8% budget deficit in 2024, EU excessive-deficit proceedings and the government’s lack of a parliamentary majority; these factors raise the risk that fiscal consolidation will be delayed, the government may fall, and France could face further rating pressure. The risk is material and could intensify around the 8 September confidence vote and scheduled Fitch, Moody’s and S&P reviews, particularly if elections produce weaker fiscal discipline: a downgrade could widen spreads further, increase refinancing costs and reduce investor appetite for French assets. Persistent bond supply, ECB quantitative tightening and substantial non-resident ownership of French government debt may add upward pressure to medium- and long-term yields, while broader eurozone contagion could amplify volatility. For real estate companies, developers, lenders and property investors, the resulting higher risk premium can make maturing loans and bond issuance more expensive, constrain access to credit, weaken valuations and increase refinancing or covenant pressure, especially for highly leveraged assets with short maturities or dependence on floating-rate debt. The outlook is not yet a sovereign crisis—Rathbones described the 78-basis-point spread as a “warning shot, but no crisis—for now”—and ABN AMRO expects spreads to stabilize or narrow if a government forms without elections and adopts some fiscal consolidation; however, an election-driven collapse could push spreads materially higher and trigger wider European spillovers. France’s weak 0.6% expected GDP growth in 2025, possible tariff-related downward revisions and only 0.4% expected construction growth reinforce a low-growth environment in which refinancing capacity should be monitored closely. TF1’s July 2025 report confirms that inflation, conflicts and macroeconomic conditions remain under close observation, although it did not model them as material risks, underscoring that the principal current signal is market-wide funding and policy uncertainty rather than a confirmed entity-specific real estate impairment.

Most Negative Sentiment Narrative - Date: 19-09-2025¶

France is receiving increasingly negative coverage for refinancing risk because political paralysis and deteriorating public finances are raising the sovereign funding benchmark that underpins domestic credit and real-estate financing. Between 26 August and 19 September 2025, the threatened collapse and eventual fall of François Bayrou’s government, uncertainty over the 2026 budget, and limited parliamentary support for the proposed €44 billion fiscal package pushed the 10-year OAT yield above 3.5%, drove the OAT-Bund spread above 80 basis points and at times toward 90–95 basis points, and lifted the 30-year yield to about 4.5%, while Fitch downgraded France from AA- to A+ on 12 September and Morningstar cited “high execution risks” for fiscal targets. The underlying severity is high: public debt is around 114–116% of GDP, the 2024 deficit was 5.8% of GDP, growth is weak, interest costs have nearly doubled since the start of the decade, and roughly 54.7–65% of government debt is held by foreign investors, leaving refinancing conditions sensitive to political and market sentiment. The principal causes are years of structural deficits, substantial welfare and pension spending, pandemic and energy-crisis support, earlier tax cuts, slow growth and, most importantly, reduced governability following the 2024 snap election; coverage increasingly compares France with eurozone “periphery” borrowers rather than core issuers. For real estate and related stakeholders, higher OAT yields raise the discount rate and refinancing cost for property companies, developers, landlords and lenders, while a sovereign downgrade can weaken French agency and bank bond ratings, widen funding spreads and reduce credit availability; banks are also vulnerable because French government debt represents a material share of Tier 1 capital. Refinancing risk could intensify as ECB quantitative tightening increases bond supply, foreign demand must absorb a large issuance burden, and pension-market reallocations may reduce demand for long-dated French debt, potentially forcing shorter maturities and more frequent refinancing. The immediate outlook is therefore elevated rather than an imminent default crisis: a stable government capable of credible consolidation could narrow spreads, but a caretaker administration, further elections or policy concessions could prolong fiscal slippage through 2027, trigger additional downgrades and push France toward a sustained risk premium. ECB support and still-orderly markets limit systemic contagion for now, yet investors should monitor the Lecornu government’s ability to pass a credible budget, OAT-Bund spreads, rating reviews, bank and covered-bond issuance costs, maturity concentration and borrowers’ interest-coverage and refinancing buffers.

Peak Volume Narrative - Date: 10-07-2025¶

Germany is receiving negative coverage indicating elevated, though largely indirect, real-estate refinancing risk as trade, fiscal, interest-rate and climate pressures weaken the economic backdrop. On 8 July 2025, “German Exports Fall Again as Tariffs Drag on Economy” reported that May’s export gains were mainly the result of temporary U.S. frontloading, while ING warned that the risk of further tariffs “hangs like a sword of Damocles over German and European exporters”; the resulting pressure on industrial activity, employment and corporate cash flows could reduce demand for property and impair borrowers’ ability to refinance. This vulnerability is compounded by higher sovereign and market funding costs: the accompanying coverage noted that Germany’s 30-year yield had risen from below zero during the pandemic to above 3%, as the country’s proposed EUR1 trillion spending plan increases borrowing needs, potentially keeping long-term financing expensive and widening refinancing gaps for leveraged developers, landlords and commercial-property owners. The risk is particularly significant because loans originated during the low-rate period may mature into a materially higher-cost environment, increasing interest burdens, valuations pressure and default or forced-sale risk, with banks and institutional investors exposed through real-estate lending and bonds. Germany’s structural weaknesses—including energy-cost shocks following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, stronger Chinese competition, the difficult green transition and political uncertainty—make a rapid recovery less certain; Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel described the economy as facing “significant headwinds in the short term.” Longer-term stress could also arise from climate events, with the ECB warning on 10 July that extreme weather could reduce euro-area GDP by almost 5% in a severe scenario, threatening asset values, insurance costs and property cash flows. Overall, the coverage signals a worsening refinancing environment rather than an immediate property-sector crisis: tariff-related weakness and persistently elevated long-term yields are the key near-term indicators to monitor, alongside debt maturities, interest coverage, refinancing spreads, vacancy and valuation trends.

Most Negative Sentiment Narrative - Date: 22-09-2025¶

Germany is receiving negative refinancing-risk coverage primarily through a macro-financial channel rather than direct evidence of property-sector distress: rising government borrowing needs, weaker economic prospects and global bond-market contagion are pushing up benchmark funding costs that influence real-estate debt pricing. On 2 September 2025, German 30-year yields reached their highest level since 2011, while coverage on 11 September cited deteriorating German confidence and renewed economic concerns; Germany’s planned increases in defence and infrastructure spending were also identified as a factor lifting borrowing costs across Europe. The ECB’s decision to hold rates and Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel’s warnings on 12 September that further cuts could “jeopardize” price stability indicate that materially cheaper refinancing may not arrive soon, with eurozone inflation at 2.1% and German fiscal stimulus potentially sustaining demand and inflation. Germany remains comparatively safer than France—French spreads exceeded 80 basis points and France was described as migrating toward the eurozone periphery—yet its own heavier debt issuance is contributing to upward pressure on long-dated yields, while weak exports and a deteriorating growth outlook raise concerns about tenants, developers and lenders’ cash flows. For commercial and residential property owners, higher benchmark rates and tighter credit margins increase refinancing costs, reduce valuations and debt-service coverage, and could force asset sales or equity injections when maturing loans are rolled over; banks and investors may also become more selective if sovereign yields continue repricing. The immediate risk appears moderate but rising rather than systemic: ECB officials said on 18 September that markets remained orderly and spreads were not yet concerning, while Fitch’s 15 September assessment that French stress had not spread to Italy, Spain or Portugal provides some containment. Key monitoring signals are the trajectory of German 10- and 30-year Bund yields, ECB policy and inflation, the scale and composition of German debt issuance, export and growth data, and evidence that property refinancing spreads or loan maturities are deteriorating faster than rental income and asset values.

Peak Volume Narrative - Date: 26-08-2025¶

Italy is receiving negative refinancing-risk coverage primarily through sovereign and financial-market channels rather than from a reported property-company default or direct real-estate refinancing event. The ESRB’s 1 August 2025 report identified Italy among EU countries subject to an excessive-deficit procedure and warned that high public debt, rising borrowing needs and increased defence spending could renew sovereign-debt sustainability concerns; this matters for real estate because higher government yields can raise banks’ funding costs, mortgage and property-investment rates, and refinancing costs for leveraged developers and landlords. Market concern intensified in the 14 August headline “French borrowing costs close in on Italy’s as investors fret over debts,” which noted that France’s 10-year yields had moved to within 0.14 percentage points of Italy’s, while Italy still carried public debt of about 140% of GDP, and in the 19 August discussion that investors were beginning to view the two sovereigns as having “similar risk profiles.” Although the convergence partly reflects worsening French fiscal and political conditions rather than a deterioration specific to Italy, it signals broader repricing of European sovereign risk and potential contagion into bank funding and credit availability. Italy’s comparatively long period of political stability and perceived fiscal prudence under Giorgia Meloni has supported lower spreads, but the underlying debt burden leaves refinancing conditions sensitive to growth, rates and investor confidence; the ESRB’s projected rise in EU debt ratios and the weak domestic growth outlook cited by Technogym on 5 August—GDP growth of only 0.2% in Q1 and 0.1% in Q2 2025—reinforce this vulnerability. The Bank of Italy Governor’s 30 July warning about global dollar concentration and interest-rate risk adds an external transmission channel, as shifts in global yields or risk appetite could tighten European financing markets. At the banking level, Euronext’s 31 July report shows substantial Italian sovereign exposure within its clearing investment portfolio and highlights the possibility that sovereign distress could affect collateral, clearing members and the wider financial system, while BFF Bank’s 8 August report demonstrates that lenders remain exposed to delayed public-sector payments and elevated non-performing classifications, despite strong liquidity and capital. Overall severity is moderate to high at the systemic refinancing level: there is no evidence here of an imminent Italian real-estate refinancing failure, but persistent fiscal pressure, weak growth, sovereign-yield volatility and possible bank-credit transmission could increase refinancing costs, reduce property valuations and heighten rollover risk, warranting close monitoring of BTP spreads, bank funding conditions, commercial-property maturities and borrower interest coverage.

Most Negative Sentiment Narrative - Date: 23-09-2025¶

Italy is receiving negative coverage primarily because elevated sovereign refinancing and fiscal-sustainability risks could spill over into domestic banks, real-estate borrowers and infrastructure assets, raising funding costs and reducing refinancing flexibility. Commerzbank’s 29 August and 22 September 2025 briefings warned that Italy’s public debt could approach 150% of GDP within ten years as low-coupon bonds are refinanced at higher rates, while aging-related spending, defense costs and rising interest payments constrain fiscal consolidation and increase the risk of a renewed sovereign-debt crisis or “fiscal dominance” of the ECB. The immediate severity is moderated by Italy’s comparatively stable government, expectations that its deficit will narrow, stronger domestic investor support and robust demand for BTPs—Tuesday’s issuance attracted EUR218 billion of bids for EUR18 billion offered—yet Italy’s BBB+ rating and high debt stock leave it vulnerable to a sharp repricing if yields rise materially or French stress triggers broader eurozone contagion. Coverage in early September noted that Italian 10-year yields around 3.68–3.71% were close to French yields, although the narrowing spread mainly reflected worsening French bonds, and that Italy was “suffering somewhat less” because of domestic demand; this relative resilience should not be mistaken for immunity. For real estate and property-linked borrowers, higher sovereign yields can transmit through bank funding, mortgage pricing, cap rates and refinancing valuations, potentially weakening collateral values, investment activity and debt-service capacity, particularly for highly leveraged assets. The refinancing signal is visible at Aeroporto Guglielmo Marconi di Bologna’s 12 September report: despite resilient passenger growth and EUR11.5 million of H1 financing cash outflows, liquidity fell to EUR22.7 million and the group moved from EUR5.4 million net cash at December 2024 to EUR17.2 million net debt at June 2025, including EUR10.5 million of short-term loans maturing in September and October ahead of a second EIB tranche; its EUR22 million investment programme and regulated tariff framework increase dependence on timely long-term funding. Overall, the risk is currently moderate but rising: stable BTP demand and ECB backstop mechanisms provide protection, while monitoring should focus on the pace of Italian yield increases, BTP demand, fiscal-consolidation credibility, bank lending conditions and the conversion of short-term infrastructure borrowing into secured long-term finance.

Peak Volume Narrative - Date: 07-07-2025¶

Greece faces an indirect but material refinancing risk from global market volatility linked to U.S. trade and fiscal policies, as reported on 7 July 2025 in “Trump’s trade policies rattle global investors” and “The euro is soaring—and Trump’s policies could push it even higher.” The euro’s more than 14% appreciation against the dollar since the start of 2025, driven by investor concerns over U.S. tariffs, attacks on the Federal Reserve, and the fiscal sustainability of the U.S. tax-and-spend law, could affect Greece through tighter or more volatile global funding conditions, exchange-rate movements, and weaker trade and investment sentiment. Central Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras warned that “those who impose tariffs will be hurt first” and attributed the dollar’s decline to the combination of tariffs, institutional tensions, and fiscal risks; the unresolved U.S.–EU trade deal adds uncertainty. The immediate severity for Greece is moderate and primarily macro-financial rather than a direct property-market shock, but sustained volatility or weaker European growth could raise refinancing costs for real-estate companies, banks, and highly leveraged borrowers, reduce investor appetite for Greek assets, and pressure property investment and valuations. The stronger euro may lower the cost of dollar-denominated imports and external debt, but it can also impair export competitiveness and complicate economic recovery. The key signal is that Greece remains exposed to externally generated funding and confidence shocks even as European assets attract safe-haven flows; monitoring sovereign and bank spreads, euro-area interest rates, commercial-property refinancing schedules, and the outcome of U.S.–EU trade negotiations is therefore warranted.

Most Negative Sentiment Narrative - Date: 22-09-2025¶

Greece is receiving negative refinancing-risk coverage primarily as a reference point in the worsening French sovereign-debt crisis, rather than because of a newly reported domestic deterioration. Between 2 and 22 September 2025, reports highlighted that France’s borrowing costs had risen to levels above Greece’s—France’s 10-year yield reached 3.555% versus Greece’s 3.427% on 22 September—and that French debt was trading at a premium associated with historically stressed euro-area borrowers. This comparison signals that Greece’s market reputation remains linked to the legacy of its sovereign crisis, while also indicating relative improvement as investors increasingly differentiate between Greek and French fiscal risk. Nevertheless, the coverage identifies meaningful contagion exposure: political instability, high debt, fiscal slippage and possible rating downgrades in France could widen spreads across Italy, Spain and Greece, raise refinancing costs, and revive eurozone debt-market fragmentation. The risk is aggravated by concerns over central-bank independence and monetary-policy credibility, after Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras warned on 26 August that attacks on Federal Reserve independence could damage the U.S. economy and have broader consequences for European policymaking. For Greece, the actionable signal is that its lower borrowing costs provide a relative buffer but do not eliminate vulnerability; renewed market stress, weaker ECB credibility or a French fiscal escalation could quickly increase sovereign refinancing costs, debt-service burdens and financing pressure for banks, property investors and other real-estate borrowers.

Peak Volume Narrative - Date: 08-09-2025¶

Spain is receiving limited negative coverage through potential eurozone financial-contagion and refinancing channels rather than from a Spain-specific real-estate shock. In its 8 September 2025 commentary, “EUR: French vote of confidence may weigh,” ING warned that French political uncertainty and a budget deficit exceeding 5% of GDP could push the French-German government bond spread above 80 basis points, increasing volatility in euro-area funding markets and potentially raising borrowing costs for banks, property companies, developers, and leveraged real-estate investors. The immediate risk is assessed as moderate and localized to France, with ING explicitly stating that it does not expect eurozone-wide stress; Spain is comparatively better positioned because it has recently benefited from sovereign upgrades, while the ECB’s Transmission Protection Instrument provides a backstop against disorderly spread widening. Nevertheless, a prolonged deterioration in French fiscal credibility, a sovereign downgrade, or broader EUR volatility could tighten refinancing conditions indirectly through higher risk premia, reduced lender appetite, and more expensive bond or bank financing, potentially pressuring property valuations and debt-service capacity. The key actionable signal is that Spain’s refinancing risk remains contained but should be monitored through Spanish sovereign spreads, bank funding costs, ECB policy, and evidence that French political stress is spilling into peripheral markets; ING’s expected EUR/USD volatility in the 1.1650–1.1750 range reinforces a cautious near-term outlook rather than a systemic Spanish real-estate refinancing event.

Most Negative Sentiment Narrative - Date: 03-10-2025¶

Spain is receiving limited negative coverage related to real-estate refinancing risk primarily through potential eurozone financial contagion rather than entity-specific property stress. On 8 September 2025, ING warned that French political instability and a possible widening of the French–German government-bond spread beyond 80 basis points could increase volatility and raise funding costs across European markets, although it considered the issue localized and noted that Italy and Spain had recently benefited from sovereign upgrades and could be supported by the ECB’s Transmission Protection Instrument. This provides Spain with a comparatively favorable sovereign backdrop, but renewed fiscal concerns elsewhere, higher long-term yields, or a broader loss of investor confidence could still increase Spanish banks’ and property borrowers’ refinancing costs, weaken debt-service capacity, and pressure commercial and residential real-estate valuations. The 30 September Northern Trust assessment further supports Spain’s relative resilience, citing strong activity even as Germany and Italy contracted, while identifying French fiscal sustainability as the main regional concern. Spain’s strong renewable-driven economic savings, reported on 3 October, may improve macroeconomic resilience, but grid gaps and post-blackout reliance on costly gas remain potential sources of volatility. Overall, current risk appears moderate and indirect: Spain is better positioned than more fiscally vulnerable peers, but real-estate refinancing conditions remain exposed to eurozone bond-market spillovers, political shocks, and any reversal in sovereign-credit sentiment.

Peak Volume Narrative - Date: 01-09-2025¶

The Netherlands is receiving negative coverage because its approximately EUR2 trillion pension-system reform could generate significant financial-market disruption and indirectly heighten real-estate refinancing risk. The transition of Europe’s largest pension system is already contributing to higher long-term bond yields and positioning for volatility in euro interest-rate swaps, while a large tranche of funds is expected to move around the turn of 2025–26 when market liquidity is lower. The Dutch central bank has warned of a financial-stability risk, although it believes the one-year transition period should allow funds to adjust portfolios orderly; market participants remain less confident, with Deutsche Bank describing early-January volatility trades as “already very crowded.” The principal causes are the scale and complexity of portfolio reallocations, hedging demands, limited transparency over market mechanics, and a wider backdrop of tariff uncertainty, fiscal concerns and political stress in France. For the Dutch real-estate sector, the key consequence is indirect but potentially material: higher and more volatile benchmark yields and swap rates could increase mortgage, development and commercial-property refinancing costs, reduce asset valuations and constrain credit availability, particularly for highly leveraged borrowers or loans maturing near the transition peak. Spillovers across European bond and funding markets could amplify these pressures, though the coverage does not identify a specific Dutch property entity or quantify direct real-estate losses. Risk monitoring should therefore focus on pension-fund transition volumes, long-dated Dutch and euro-area yields, swap-market liquidity, lender refinancing terms and refinancing concentrations around year-end and early January.

Most Negative Sentiment Narrative - Date: 28-09-2025¶

The Netherlands is receiving negative coverage because its planned near-EUR2 trillion pension reform could create significant refinancing and financial-stability pressure across European bond and swap markets, with indirect but material implications for real-estate borrowers. The 1 September 2025 Bloomberg report, “A EUR2 Trillion Dutch Pension Headache Is Coming for European Bonds,” said the transition was already lifting longer-dated bond yields and prompting hedging activity in euro swaps, while a large year-end tranche and thinner liquidity could intensify volatility; the Dutch central bank had warned of financial-stability risks, even as it considered the one-year transition period sufficient for orderly portfolio adjustments. Higher long-term yields and disrupted swap markets can raise financing costs, reduce debt-service capacity, complicate refinancing of commercial property and development loans, and weaken asset valuations, particularly for leveraged owners and lenders dependent on stable capital markets. The risk is most acute around the turn of the year, when trading desks expect front-loaded repositioning and “volatility trades in early January are already very crowded,” creating potential spillovers beyond Dutch pensions into wider European credit markets. Broader concerns reinforce the adverse outlook: on 17 September, ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone cited geopolitical fragmentation, cyber risk and climate losses as threats to financial resilience, while on 28 September Dutch central-bank chief Klaas Sleijpen warned that ECB tools cannot resolve Europe’s fiscal problems and questioned renewed quantitative easing because of its effects on financial stability. Overall, the coverage signals elevated, market-driven refinancing risk rather than evidence of an immediate Dutch property crisis; key indicators to monitor are long-term Dutch and European yields, euro-swap liquidity, pension-transition flows, lender refinancing spreads, and the ability of real-estate borrowers to extend or hedge maturing debt.

Peak Volume Narrative - Date: 05-08-2025¶

Portugal faces an indirect but meaningful refinancing risk in real estate as weak business investment and persistent policy uncertainty weigh on economic growth and financing conditions. The 5 August 2025 coverage, “Weak business investment threatens global growth, warns OECD,” reports that investment across the OECD remains 20% below the level implied by pre-financial-crisis trends and 6.7% below the pre-Covid trend, while global growth is expected to slow to 3% in 2025 from 3.3% in 2024. Although the article does not identify a Portugal-specific property stress event, the conditions are relevant to Portuguese real estate because subdued investment can weaken corporate cash flows, employment, property demand and lenders’ willingness to refinance maturing loans. The stated cause is “pervasive” policy uncertainty, compounded by repeated macroeconomic and trade shocks; this may encourage banks and investors to demand higher margins, shorter maturities or stronger collateral, increasing rollover pressure for leveraged developers, landlords and commercial property owners. Severity is currently moderate and primarily macro-financial rather than evidence of an immediate default wave, but the risk could intensify if slower growth coincides with elevated interest rates, falling valuations or tighter credit. The actionable signal is that borrowers and lenders should stress-test refinancing needs against weaker growth and more conservative funding terms, while monitoring investment trends, bank risk appetite and policy developments for signs that Portugal’s real estate refinancing environment is deteriorating.

Most Negative Sentiment Narrative - Date: 16-09-2025¶

Portugal’s refinancing risk in real estate appears moderate rather than acute, with the 16 September 2025 ING coverage indicating that sovereign upgrades for Portugal are offsetting concerns over French political instability and supporting euro-area market sentiment. The improved sovereign outlook should help contain Portuguese borrowing costs and preserve access to funding for property owners, developers, and lenders, while the eurozone rate environment is becoming less supportive of further relief as markets increasingly expect the ECB to have finished cutting at 2.00%; this could limit the reduction in refinancing costs for loans rolling over from higher-rate periods. The broader macroeconomic backdrop remains fragile, including weak consumer confidence, fiscal pressures, and trade imbalances cited in the 5 September coverage, which could weigh on property demand, rental affordability, valuations, and borrowers’ repayment capacity if growth deteriorates. Compared with France, Portugal is benefiting from stronger fiscal credibility and sovereign-rating momentum, reducing immediate refinancing stress, but elevated rates and uncertain economic conditions still warrant monitoring of highly leveraged real-estate borrowers, short-maturity debt, interest coverage, and exposure to weaker household or commercial-property cash flows.

Peak Volume Narrative - Date: 05-07-2025¶

Ireland’s refinancing risk in real estate is not directly evidenced in the 5 July 2025 coverage, but ECB Governing Council member and Central Bank of Ireland Governor Gabriel Makhlouf’s comments that the euro is not yet ready to challenge the dollar highlight a relevant macro-financial vulnerability. Europe’s lack of a unified fiscal capacity and a common safe asset comparable to US Treasuries may constrain the depth and resilience of euro-area funding markets, particularly during periods of stress. For Irish property borrowers, developers, lenders, and investors, this could translate into higher or more volatile refinancing costs and reduced access to liquidity if global investors favor dollar assets or risk aversion increases. The immediate severity is indirect and uncertain, with no specific Irish real-estate defaults, maturities, or funding pressures cited, but the statement signals that external monetary and sovereign-market conditions remain important drivers of refinancing risk. Stakeholders should therefore monitor euro-area bond spreads, bank lending standards, currency movements, and the rollover profile of highly leveraged property exposures.

Most Negative Sentiment Narrative - Date: 01-08-2025¶

Ireland faces a moderate and still evolving real-estate refinancing risk driven primarily by macroeconomic and market uncertainty rather than evidence of an immediate property-sector crisis. The ECB’s eight rate cuts over the prior year have reduced borrowing costs and eased near-term refinancing pressure, but the 1 August 2025 report, “Euro zone inflation holds at 2%, backing ECB caution on rates,” indicates that further easing is now uncertain: Governor Gabriel Makhlouf said policymakers had reached a point where they could “wait and see,” while investors priced in less than a 50% chance of another cut. This creates a risk for property owners, developers and lenders refinancing debt at potentially higher rates than originally expected, particularly where maturities are concentrated or assets depend on aggressive valuations and rental or sales growth. The 9 July coverage of threatened US tariffs adds a second vulnerability, as ECB analysis warned that persistent 10% duties and higher tariffs on steel and cars could produce a “significant slow down” in Europe, with spillover from US measures against Asia; weaker growth could reduce occupier demand, construction activity, investment and borrowers’ ability to service or refinance loans. Longer-term financial fragmentation is also relevant: on 5 July, Makhlouf said the euro is not yet ready to challenge the dollar because Europe lacks a unified fiscal capacity and a safe asset comparable to US Treasuries, potentially limiting the depth and resilience of euro-area funding markets during stress. Overall, lower rates and contained inflation provide some refinancing relief, but a pause in monetary easing, tariff-driven growth risks and structural limitations in European capital markets warrant close monitoring of debt maturities, interest-rate hedges, loan-to-value ratios, liquidity buffers and exposure to weaker commercial-property demand.

Peak Volume Narrative - Date: 10-07-2025¶

Belgium receives limited and indirect negative coverage related to real-estate refinancing risk in the 10 July 2025 ECB Working Paper “Monetary policy transmission through cross-selling banks,” which is explicitly research by the authors and not an official ECB view. The paper finds that banks may offer lower deposit spreads to attract and retain customers when future cross-selling of loans is valuable, particularly when policy rates are low; this can influence funding costs, deposit competition, and the transmission of monetary policy. Although the extract does not identify Belgian property-market stress, defaults, or refinancing shortfalls, the mechanism is relevant to real-estate borrowers because changes in bank funding conditions and policy-rate transmission affect mortgage pricing, loan availability, and the ability of households and property companies to refinance. The main risk is therefore systemic and forward-looking rather than evidence of an immediate Belgium-specific crisis: if banks face weaker margins, tighter liquidity, or reassess the value of future lending relationships, refinancing terms could become less favorable and expose highly leveraged borrowers to repayment pressure. The involvement of the National Bank of Belgium in the ChaMP network underscores the relevance of the research to Belgian monetary and banking conditions, while the paper’s broader context—unprecedented shocks, structural change, and the reversal of the inflation surge—signals continued uncertainty around interest-rate transmission. Stakeholders should monitor deposit competition, bank lending standards, mortgage repricing, and refinancing maturities, but the available extract supports a moderate analytical concern rather than a confirmed elevated real-estate refinancing event.

Most Negative Sentiment Narrative - Date: 03-09-2025¶

Belgium is facing heightened refinancing risk indirectly through worsening sovereign and regional bond-market conditions, as highlighted in the 3 September 2025 coverage, “Europe’s Bond Market Selloff: What’s Happening?” Rising public debt, higher borrowing costs, and pressure to fund defense and infrastructure are eroding fiscal flexibility across Europe, while political uncertainty—described by ING Belgium economist Charlotte de Montpellier as creating “fresh uncertainty” in an already fragile landscape and with the parliamentary vote obstacle “almost impossible to overcome”—could further undermine investor confidence. Although the article does not identify a Belgium-specific property-market shock, wider sovereign-spread volatility can raise banks’ funding costs and translate into more expensive or less available refinancing for Belgian developers, landlords, and highly leveraged commercial real-estate borrowers, particularly where loans mature in the near term or rely on variable rates. The risk is moderate but increasing: persistent fiscal concerns and global debt expansion, alongside elevated government yields elsewhere in Europe, could tighten credit, depress valuations, delay transactions, and increase default or restructuring pressure for weaker property owners. Key signals to monitor are Belgium’s political and budget outcomes, sovereign-yield spreads, bank lending standards, refinancing pipelines, and the ability of real-estate borrowers to extend maturities or reduce leverage before market conditions deteriorate further.

Peak Volume Narrative - Date: 06-08-2025¶

Austria is exposed to heightened real-estate refinancing risk through the broader deterioration in global macroeconomic and financial conditions highlighted on 6 August 2025 in “Global Trade Is More Fragmented, Fed Is Lost, World Heads for New Era of Uncertainty.” The extract points to fragmented trade, weakening US economic data, uncertain capital flows, and a widening US–eurozone policy divergence, with ECB Governing Council member Robert Holzmann warning against further rate cuts because of financial-stability concerns and still-high inflation. Although it does not identify an Austria-specific property or borrower event, these conditions are relevant because prolonged or volatile euro-area borrowing costs can increase refinancing expenses, reduce property valuations and debt-service capacity, and make lenders more selective when maturing commercial real-estate loans are rolled over. Austrian developers, landlords and highly leveraged investors could therefore face margin compression, refinancing gaps, forced asset sales or reduced investment, with consequences for banks and wider financial stability if defaults rise. The immediate risk signal is elevated uncertainty rather than a confirmed deterioration in Austria’s property sector; however, the conflicting central-bank outlook and more fragmented trade environment argue for close monitoring of loan maturities, floating-rate exposure, interest-coverage ratios, collateral values and access to alternative funding.

Most Negative Sentiment Narrative - Date: 15-09-2025¶

Austria’s refinancing risk in real estate is indirectly elevated by a tighter-for-longer euro-area interest-rate outlook and volatile sovereign-credit conditions. In the 15 September 2025 report “Euro zone bond yields steady; France dented by downgrade,” newly appointed Austrian central-bank governor Martin Kocher said the ECB was “at, or very close, to the end of its easing cycle,” suggesting that further declines in borrowing costs—and associated relief for property owners refinancing loans—may be limited. Although the article does not identify an Austria-specific downgrade or property-market stress, increased government debt issuance across Europe, including €28 billion of planned auctions, and political and rating uncertainty surrounding France could keep regional bond yields and credit spreads volatile. For Austrian real-estate borrowers, this raises the severity of refinancing exposure as maturing debt may need to be rolled over at materially higher rates than during the low-rate period, pressuring interest coverage, valuations, development activity, and lenders’ asset quality. The key actionable signal is that refinancing assumptions should remain conservative: entities with near-term maturities, floating-rate debt, high leverage, or dependence on continued ECB easing are particularly vulnerable, while sustained yield stability or renewed rate cuts would be necessary to ease the risk.
